sentences.text:
Order 
Appellant has preferred this criminal appeal under Section 378 of Cr.P.C. after obtaining leave vide order dated 17.4.2006 from this Court under Section 378(4) of Cr.P.C. against the impugned judgment of acquittal dated 3.1.2005 passed by Judicial Magistrate First Class, Vidisha in Criminal Case No.148/2004 for offence under Sections 16(1)(a)(i)(ii) of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act,
1954 (in short PFA Act).
2.
As per prosecution story on 15.5.1998 Food Inspector Ram Singh along with S.N. Verma inspected the Shreshti Sweets and found that the respondent was selling several sweets along with curd.
Food Inspector disclosed his identity, gave notice to the respondent/accused and purchased 600 Gm. curd after paying Rs.12.50.
He disclosed that the sample would be sent for analysis.

Food Inspector divided the sample into three equal parts and added 48 drops of formalin in each part and kept the sample in dry and NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 2 CRA-303-2006 clean glass.
Bottle was sealed on the spot.
The spot map was also prepared.
One bottle of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst.
Public Analyst found that the same was found adulterated and unfit for human consumption.
On receipt of the report of Public Analyst, the Food Inspector obtained sanction.
It is also found that respondent/accused was selling the aforesaid product without having any valid license for its trade.

Copy of report of analyst was also sent along with the memorandum to the respondent/accused by the registered post at his address in compliance of provision of Section 13(2) of PFA Act and thereafter complaint has been filed before the Trial Court.

1 3. The Trial Court framed the charges under Section 7(1), 7(5) r/w Section 16(1)(a)(i)(ii) of PFA Act.

sentences.text: The appellant abjured his guilt and pleaded complete innocence.
4. Prosecution has examined as many as three witnesses while respondent/accused has examined one defence witness.

5. The Trial Court after due appreciation of entire evidence available on record came to the conclusion that the prosecution has failed to establish that the charges framed against the respondent/accused is beyond reasonable doubt and by the impugned order, acquitted the respondent from all the aforesaid charges.
Being aggrieved by the acquittal of the respondent

,
appellant has preferred this appeal.

6. Learned Pubic Prosecutor for the appellant submits that the Trial Court has not properly appreciated the oral as well as documentary evidence available on record and wrongly acquitted the respondent/accused from the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 3 CRA-303-2006 charges leveled against him.

7. Considered the submissions made by counsel for the appellant.
8.
The case of prosecution before the Trial Court was that the respondent/accused was selling the adulterated curd.

In that regard if the material available on record is perused, it becomes clear that as per provisions of Rule 14 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 which is mandatory in nature, food Inspector at the time of taking the sample has to take care that the container/utensil in which he intends to take the sample is properly washed, dried and does not contain any colour or odur and not only that, the prosecution has to establish, at the time of trial, that the provisions of Rule 14 are complied with.

But in the present case, the complainant, Food Inspector Ram Singh (PW-1), nowhere in his evidence stated that as and when and in whose presence he had cleaned the container / utensil used in taking the disputed sample, therefore, the case of prosecution appears to be doubtful.
9.

Learned counsel for the respondent/accused before the Trial Court has forcefully contended that in view Section 13 of PFA Act, the report of Public Analyst has become inadmissible in evidence is a just and proper because it is not made clear during the sample process or in the complaint that the curd was made from milk of cow or buffalo.
Even in the Public Analyst report Ex.P/21 nothing is mentioned adulterated.
Therefore, on the basis of aforesaid, report of the Public Analyst is not appears to be just and proper.

Apart from the above, it is also mentioned that the prosecution has examined Mulayam Chand (PW-2) who has not supported the statement of NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 4 CRA-303-2006 Food Inspector Ram Singh.
Ram Singh categorically stated that at the time of incident, Food Inspector S.N. Verma was with him but S.N.Verma was not examined by the prosecution before the Trial Court.
Non-examination of the material witness is fatal for the prosecution.
Apart from above, it is also noteworthy that respondent/accused has taken plea that he is not proprietor of the aforesaid shop and he is a practicing lawyer.
Food Inspector Ram Singh (PW-1) in his cross-examination admits that he did not file any relevant document regarding the ownership/proprietor ship of the aforesaid shop.

sentences.text:
Defence witness Bhagwan Das (DW-1) also deposed that owner of the shop is Udaipal and respondent/accused is not owner of the aforesaid shop and he never run the aforesaid shop,
therefore, prosecution also failed to prove that the respondent/accused is proprietor of the aforesaid shop.

11. Therefore, from perusal of oral as well as documentary evidence lead before the Trial Court, this Court is of the considered opinion that the Trial Court while considering the evidence available on record has clearly observed that the prosecution has not followed the mandatory provisions during the sealing and seizing the sample, therefore, the prosecution has failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt and whole case of the prosecution is doubtful.
Even in the present appeal, nothing is produced or pointed out to rebut the conclusion of the Trial Court.

Thus, from the evidence itself,
it is established that the prosecution has not proved his case beyond reasonable doubt.
12.

In the case of State of M.P. vs. Arvind Joshi reported in 2008 NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 5 CRA-303-2006 (2) Crimes 228 (M.P.), this Court has held as under:
"10.

2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 5 CRA-303-2006 (2) Crimes 228 (M.P.)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, the court has found that the prosecution has failed to prove the charges and allegations against the respondent by producing evidence beyond reasonable doubt.

After considering the evidence as well as the findings of the trial court, we are also of the view that the prosecution evidence is doubtful and with a firmness it cannot be held that the evidence of all the remaining three eye-witnesses is reliable or that they made the truthful version of the incident or narrated the story correctly in the court or that the findings of acquittal are liable to be reversed merely on their evidence.
According to us, the trial court has not committed any illegality in recording the findings of acquittal against the respondent.

11. It is settled principle under law that normally unless the finding of acquittal is totally perverse and wholly unreasonable, the appellate court should not interfere in the finding of acquittal simply on the ground that other views is also possible from the same set of evidence.

12. In a case of State of Goa vs. Sanjay Thakran and Anr. (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 162 the Hon. Supreme Court has held that: "While exercising the powers in an appeal against the order of acquittal the court of appeal would not ordinarily interfere with the order of acquittal unless the approach of the lower court is vitiated by some manifest illegality and the conclusion arrived at would not be arrived at by any reasonable person and, therefore, the decision is to be characterized as perverse.

entities.text: State of Goa vs. Sanjay Thakran and Anr. (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 162
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Merely because two views are possible, the court of appeal would not take the view, which would upset the judgment delivered by the court below.

However, the appellate court has a power to review the evidence if it is of the view that the view arrived at by the court below is perverse and the court has committed a manifest error of law and ignored the material evidence on record.

A duty is cast upon the appellate court, in such circumstances, to re appreciate the evidence to arrive at a just decision on the basis of material placed on record to find out whether any of the accused is connected with State Of M.P. vs Dinesh Singh on 25 June, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117475600/
3 commission of the crime he is charged with."

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
13. In a case of Peerappaand Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2006) 1 SCC (Cri) 586, their Lordships recalled the observations made by His Lordship of the Supreme Court, in a case of Kashiram v. State of M.P. (2002) 1 SCC 71, as observed, thus: "Though the High Court while hearing an appeal against an acquittal has powers as wide and comprehensive as in an appeal against a conviction and while exercising its appellate jurisdiction the High Court can reappraise the evidence, arrive at findings at variance with those recorded by the trial court in its order of acquittal and arrive at its own findings,
yet, the salutary principle which would guide the High Court is -if two views are reasonable possible,
one supporting the acquittal and the other recording a conviction, the High Court would not interfere merely because it feels that sitting as a trial court its view would have been one of recording a NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:12809 6 CRA-303-2006 conviction.

entities.text: Peerappaand Ors. v. State of Karnataka (2006) 1 SCC (Cri) 586
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Kashiram v. State of M.P. (2002) 1 SCC 71
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It follows as a necessary corollary that it is obligatory on the High Court while reversing an order of acquittal to consider and discuss each of the reasons given by the trial court to acquit the accused and then to dislodge those reasons.
Failure to discharge this obligation constitutes a serious infirmity in the judgment of the High Court.
That obligation has not been discharged by the High Court in the instant case.
On the reasons given by the trial court while appreciating the evidence have not been dealt with by the High Court."

13. Now, so far as the present appeal against the judgment of acquittal is concerned, it is settled law that High Court would not ordinarily interfere with the order of acquittal unless the approach of the lower appellate Court is vitiated by some manifest illegality

. Merely because two views are possible,
the High Court would not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the Trial Court as held in the decision of State of M.P. Vs. Ramcharan and others, 1985 MPLJ 714.
14.

entities.text: State of M.P. Vs. Ramcharan and others, 1985 MPLJ 714
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Taking this view of the matter, no interference is called for in the judgment of acquittal dated 3.1.2005 passed by the Trial Court.
Accordingly, the appeal preferred by the State is accordingly dismissed.
15. The respondent is on bail.
His bail bonds shall stand discharged.
(ANIL VERMA) JUDGE (alok)
